quests.hint: The joint in the middle of your leg. It begins with a letter you never say.
quests.explanation: The kn- at the start of a word is pronounced /n/: knee, knife, knock, know. The k is silent, though it once was spoken. The vowel team ee is the usual spelling here.

quests.hint: Not correct. It opens with a consonant pair whose first letter is silent.
quests.explanation: Words that start with wr- say only /r/: wrong, wrist, wrap, write. The w is not pronounced, so it is easy to leave out in fast typing.

quests.hint: A board on a road or a shop. Between the vowel and the final n, there is a letter you don't hear.
quests.explanation: The g in sign is silent, but it comes back in related words such as signal and signature. Relatives can help you find a hidden letter.

quests.hint: To go up a hill or a ladder. The last letter is written but not spoken.
quests.explanation: After m at the end of a word, b is often silent: climb, comb, lamb, thumb. The b reveals nothing to the ear, so it has to be memorised.

quests.hint: Feeling unsure. A silent consonant sits between the vowel and the final t.
quests.explanation: Doubt has a silent b before the t. Scholars added the b long ago to show the word's Latin origin (dubitare), even though it is not pronounced.

quests.hint: Money that you owe. It has the same silent letter, in the same place, as 'doubt'.
quests.explanation: Debt has a silent b before t, like doubt. The b comes from Latin debitum, and it returns in the related word 'debit'.

quests.hint: To pay attention with your ears. The t in the middle doesn't sound.
quests.explanation: In -sten words, the t is silent: listen, fasten, glisten. The same silent t appears in castle and whistle, where it follows an s.

quests.hint: Fifty percent. A letter in the middle is written but not pronounced.
quests.explanation: In half, calf, talk, walk and calm, an l sits silently after a. Half also changes its f to v in the plural: halves.

quests.hint: The season after summer. The last letter isn't spoken.
quests.explanation: A final n after m is silent in autumn, column and hymn. The n reappears in related forms such as 'autumnal', which is a useful clue.

quests.hint: Sixty minutes. It starts with a letter you don't say, and the vowel sounds like 'ow'.
quests.explanation: Hour has a silent h, like honest and heir. The sound is the same as our, but the spelling starts with h.

quests.hint: A spirit in a story. The first sound, /g/, is written with two letters.
quests.explanation: Most words treat gh as silent (night) or /f/ (enough), but at the start of ghost, it says /g/. The odd spelling is generally traced to early printers.

quests.hint: The beat of music or speech. It contains no a, e, i, o or u.
quests.explanation: Rhythm has y as its only vowel. Its rh comes from Greek, and it has two h's, one near the start and one inside the th. Dropping the first h gives 'rythm', which is wrong.

quests.hint: Someone you like and trust. The vowel sounds like /e/ but is written with two letters, i first.
quests.explanation: Friend has ie, but the sound is /e/. A memory aid: a friend is with you to the end, and the word ends in -end.

quests.hint: To get something sent to you. After c, the long e is spelled ei.
quests.explanation: After c, the /iː/ sound is usually ei: receive, deceive, ceiling. The 'i before e' rhyme is reliable only for that sound and only when a c comes first.

quests.hint: Strange. The long e is spelled ei, and there is no c before it.
quests.explanation: Weird breaks the 'i before e' rhyme, as do seize and either. These have to be memorised as exceptions.

quests.hint: Apart, not together. The middle of the word has a short three-letter chunk that rhymes with 'cat'.
quests.explanation: Sep-a-rate: the second syllable has an a. An e in the second syllable gives 'seperate', which is wrong. The last syllable is written -rate, whether it is a verb or an adjective.

quests.hint: Without a doubt. It contains the word 'finite', spelled the same way.
quests.explanation: Definite ends in -ite. Add -ly with no change: definitely. Writing 'definately' is very common, but it breaks the pattern.

quests.hint: Needed. It has fewer c's than s's.
quests.explanation: Ne-ces-sar-y has one c and a double s. A memory aid is one collar, two sleeves. Doubling the c gives 'neccessary', which is wrong.

quests.hint: To make someone feel awkward in public. It has two pairs of doubled letters.
quests.explanation: Em-bar-rass has rr and ss. Say it in syllables and look for both doubles, since the sound of the word doesn't give either one away.

quests.hint: A particular time or event. It opens with a doubled letter and has a single s later.
quests.explanation: Occasion has cc and a single s, and -sion says /ʒən/. The related word occasionally keeps the same cc and s, and adds ll.

quests.hint: To suggest that something is good. It has a single c and a double m.
quests.explanation: Re + commend: the base commend gives the mm, and the prefix re- adds nothing extra. Doubling the c gives 'reccomend', which is wrong.

quests.hint: As much as needed. The ending sounds like f.
quests.explanation: The letters ough can say /ʌf/, as in enough, tough and rough. The sound of the ending doesn't tell you the spelling, so learn the word in one piece.

quests.hint: The reply to a question. A letter in the middle isn't pronounced.
quests.explanation: The w in answer is silent, as in sword. The word comes from Old English and-swaru, in which the w was once spoken.

quests.hint: Land surrounded by water. The second letter isn't pronounced.
quests.explanation: The s in island is silent. It was inserted centuries ago by writers who thought the word came from Latin insula. In fact it is from Old English.

quests.hint: How hot or cold it is. The word contains a short syllable that speakers usually skip.
quests.explanation: Tem-per-a-ture has four written syllables, though many people say three. The a after per is silent in fast speech but must be written; the ending is -ture.

quests.hint: A food plant such as a carrot or a cabbage. Speakers often say three syllables, but four are written.
quests.explanation: Veg-e-ta-ble is usually said as VEJ-tuh-bul, so the second vowel disappears in speech. It is still written, and the ending is -able.

quests.hint: A place full of books. The first r is often dropped when people say it.
quests.explanation: Li-brar-y has an r after the b and another after the a. The word comes from Latin liber (book). Skipping the second r gives 'libary'.

quests.hint: A place to eat out. It has a vowel pair in the second syllable that speakers often shorten.
quests.explanation: Res-tau-rant has the letters au, and it ends in -ant. Speakers often say two syllables, which hides the middle vowels.

quests.hint: A promise about quality. A u follows the g, and the ending has a double vowel.
quests.explanation: After g, a u can be written to keep the g hard: guarantee, guard, guess. The ending is -ee, as in agree.

quests.hint: A special right or advantage. It ends in -ege, and people often add a d.
quests.explanation: Priv-i-lege is spelled with -lege and no d, even though the sound at the end is /dʒ/. Adding a d gives 'priviledge', which is wrong.
